newsitem.title: INDIA: India sees rise in soymeal prices.
newsitem.headline: India sees rise in soymeal prices.

text.p: Indian exporters have signed contracts for up to 225,000 tonnes of soymeal for shipment in November and December, and expect prices to firm up further this month, officials and traders said on Friday.

"Nearly 225,000 tonnes of soymeal have been committed so far for November-December shipments. It is a rough estimation," Davish Jain, said chairman of the Soybean Processors Association of India (SOPA).
Jain told Reuters that overseas sales for the new crop started from $240 FAS (free alongside ship) per tonne. Traders were currently signing deals at $265-270, he said.
"The market is bullish. The processors expect the prices to go up to $285-290 per tonne this month," said Sunil Saboo, a leading oilmeal broker.
Industry officials said they expect India to export about 2.2-2.5 million tonnes of soymeal in 1996/97 (November-October).
Soymeal exports in 1995/96 were expected to be about 2.6 million tonnes, higher than the earlier estimate of 2.4 million.
Saboo said selling on Thursday was on small volumes after prices at the Chicago market fell. "Buyers started quoting lower but there were no aggresive sellers," he said.
"We expect around 10,000 tonnes of soymeal sales at $275 per tonne on Friday," Saboo added.
He said China and Malaysia were in the market to buy but traders were not specifying the destinations.
"The cost and freight prices would depend on the destination. We are doing 90 percent of our sales on FAS basis," Saboo said.
Traders said purchases were being made on behalf of China, Indonesia, Japan, Malaysia and Korea.
"Major sales are being done through multinational houses and their counterparts. The destinations are not known," Jain said.
He said demand for Indian soymeal was good and the market showed a healthy trend.
"A lot will depend on the U.S. crop due in a couple of months. Our share is only seven or eight percent in the meal market," Jain said.

Indian industry had set a soybean production target of 4.5 million tonnes for 1996/97. But erratic weather conditions delayed sowing in central Madhya Pradesh state, which accounts for nearly 80 percent of the country's soybean production.
Traders had said this could delay the harvest, and the yields might be nearly 20 percent below target.
"There is nothing to show a weak market. We may have reasonably good prices this season," Jain said.
